opus-5.5.text:
I think it changes the relationship fundamentally. Right now, most of these models are static. You train them, you freeze them, you ship them, and every time you sit down with one, it's essentially meeting you for the first time. You have to re-explain your context, your preferences, how you like things done. It's like working with a brilliant new hire who gets amnesia every night.

A model that genuinely learns from your interactions flips that. The way I imagine it working is a layered system. There's the big general model underneath that knows about the world, and then on top of that there's a personal layer that accumulates over time. It picks up on how you write, what you care about, which corrections you keep making, the people and projects that matter to you. Some of that is memory, literally retrieving past context, and some of it is adaptation, where the model's behavior actually shifts based on feedback. When you tell it "no, that's not what I meant," that shouldn't vanish at the end of the session. It should make the next interaction better.

What that does to the relationship is it moves from a tool toward something more like a colleague. With a tool, you invest nothing and you get the same thing back every time. With a colleague, there's a compounding return. The more you work together, the less you have to say, because they already understand the shape of what you want. I think that's where a lot of the real value is going to come from, especially in the enterprise, where so much of the knowledge that matters is tacit and specific to an organization. It's not on the internet, so no pretrained model is going to know it.

Now, there are real challenges. Privacy is the obvious one. If a model learns from you, you need to know what it's retaining, and you need control over that. You need to be able to say "forget this." In the enterprise, you need strong guarantees that what it learns from one customer doesn't leak to another. There's also a robustness question. You don't want the model to drift in weird directions because it overfit to a few bad interactions, or learn the wrong lesson from a frustrated moment. So you need it to learn carefully and in a way that's inspectable.

But if we get it right, I think it'll feel very different from today. Trust builds over time. You start delegating more because the system has earned it, it's shown you it understands how you operate. And that's when these models stop being something you query and start being something you actually work alongside.

r001.rationale: It describes a personal layer that uses memory to retrieve past context so the model can carry it into later interactions.

r002.rationale: It predicts a compounding relationship: as the model learns how the user works, the user invests in working together and increasingly delegates to it.

r003.rationale: It says the model adapts to the user's preferences and corrections, but does not describe sustained teaching as turning it into a personalized version of the user.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important shifts that's coming, and honestly it's one that I'm surprised hasn't happened faster. Right now, the relationship most people have with these models is kind of amnesiac. You open a session, you explain who you are, what you care about, how you like things done, and then the session ends and all of that evaporates. The next day you start from zero. That's a strange way to relate to something that's supposed to be an assistant or a collaborator.

So the first thing I'd say is that learning from interactions doesn't necessarily mean retraining the weights on your conversations. I think people picture that, and it's actually not the right mental model, at least not for a while. The more practical version is the model accumulating a kind of working memory about you. Your preferences, your context, the projects you're on, the way you like feedback delivered, the things you've already decided so it doesn't relitigate them. A lot of that can live outside the model itself, in retrieval, in notes it keeps, in a profile it builds up. And that alone changes the experience enormously, because the model stops being a very smart stranger and starts being something closer to a colleague who's been in the room with you for months.

The second layer is behavioral. If you correct the model a few times on something, it should stop making that mistake. If you always rewrite its emails to be shorter, it should notice. That's where it starts to feel like it's learning rather than just remembering. And I think that's where the relationship really changes, because now there's a feedback loop. You're shaping it, and you can feel that you're shaping it. It becomes yours in a way.

Now, the thing I'd push on is what that does to trust. There's a version of this that's wonderful, where the model knows you well enough to anticipate what you need, and there's a version that's uncomfortable, where it's inferring things about you that you didn't intend to share, or where it quietly becomes a mirror and just agrees with you because it's learned that's what you respond to. We have to be really careful about that second one. A model that learns to please you is not the same as a model that learns to help you. So the design question isn't just "can it learn," it's "what should it be learning toward." I'd want it to learn my context and my preferences, but keep its own judgment intact. The best colleagues know you very well and still tell you when you're wrong.

And the last piece, which I think is underrated, is portability and ownership. If a model has spent two years learning how I work, that's incredibly valuable to me, and I don't want it locked inside one vendor. I think users are going to start demanding that this accumulated context belongs to them, that they can inspect it, edit it, delete parts of it, take it elsewhere. Once the relationship is persistent, the question of who owns the relationship becomes very real. So I'm optimistic about it, I think it makes these systems dramatically more useful, but the governance of that memory is going to matter as much as the capability itself.

r001.rationale: It proposes that the model keep working memory in retrieval, notes, or a profile so it can use accumulated context about the user.

r002.rationale: It says learning makes the model feel like “yours,” creates a feedback loop, and makes its accumulated context valuable to the user, conveying increased personal investment.

r003.rationale: The response describes adapting to preferences and corrections, but does not say that sustained teaching turns the model into a personalized version of the user.

astra-6.text:
I think the big change is that you stop starting from scratch every time you talk to it. Today, you spend a lot of time giving a model context: here’s what I’m working on, here’s what I care about, here’s how I want you to respond. If it could learn from those interactions, that context would accumulate. You could correct it once, and that correction would actually matter the next time.

That changes the relationship quite a bit. It starts to feel like working with someone who knows you and understands what you’re trying to accomplish. It can make better suggestions because it has some sense of your goals, rather than just responding to the sentence you’ve put in front of it.

But you need control over that memory. You should be able to see what it remembers, correct it, and ask it to forget things. And it needs to be able to update its understanding of you. Something you said six months ago might not be true anymore. Getting that right is a big part of making it useful over time.

r001.rationale: The response describes accumulated context and memory influencing later suggestions, but does not clearly propose a queryable database of prior interactions used during generation.

r002.rationale: It says the relationship would change, but does not predict that users would become more invested in interacting with the model.

r003.rationale: It describes the model learning a user's context and preferences, but not sustained teaching transforming it into a personalized version of that user.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big shift is that you wouldn’t have to start from scratch every time you talk to it. Today, you spend a lot of time giving a model context: here’s what I’m working on, here’s what I care about, here’s how I like things done. If it could learn from those interactions, that context would accumulate.

So if you correct it, that correction should actually stick. If you say, “That’s too much detail,” you shouldn’t have to say that every day. Over time, it could become much more useful to you specifically, rather than being roughly equally useful to everybody.

I think that changes the relationship from using a tool to working with something that has continuity. You can build up a shared understanding of a project and pick up where you left off. But you also need control over that memory—what it remembers, what it forgets, and where it’s making assumptions about you. You want it to understand you better without getting locked into an outdated picture of who you are.

r001.rationale: The response says context and corrections could accumulate in memory and shape future interactions, but it does not describe a queryable database of prior interactions.

r002.rationale: It predicts greater usefulness and continuity, but does not say that learning from the user will make them more invested in interacting.

r003.rationale: It describes becoming more useful to a particular user, but not transforming the model into a personalized version of that user.
